# Home Assignment: Battleship

**Time estimate:** ~45 minutes

## The Task

Build a **Battleship** game as a full-stack web application. Two players, each with a **6x6 board** and **3 ships** (sizes: 2, 3, 4). Players place their ships, then take turns firing at each other's board. First to sink all opponent ships wins.

- **FastAPI** backend that manages the game: board state, ship placement validation, turn logic, hit/miss/sunk detection. Expose REST endpoints for placing ships, firing shots, and viewing boards. Important: a player should never see the opponent's ship positions — only their own hits and misses.
- **MCP tool server** ([Python SDK](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk)) running over **Streamable HTTP** that exposes the same game actions as tools — so an AI agent could play the game.
- **Vue 3** frontend that shows both grids (your board + your attack view of the opponent), lets you place ships and fire shots. Only Player 1 needs UI controls — Player 2 can be idle for now.
- **Docker Compose** with all services containerized. Each service can expose its own port.

A single `docker compose up --build` should bring everything up.

## Deliverables

1. Source code (Git repo or zip) with a `docker-compose.yml` at the root
2. A brief `README.md` explaining how to run the project

## What We're Looking For

Clean, readable code. A working game. Correct use of FastAPI, Vue, and MCP. Solid Docker setup. Design decisions are yours — we'll discuss them in the follow-up.

## Not Required

Persistent storage, authentication, tests, polished UI.

## Follow-Up Session (~30 minutes)

After submission we'll do a live session: walk through your solution, debug together, extend the app with a new feature, and discuss architecture trade-offs. Come ready to share your screen.

Good luck, have fun!

architecture.style: Modular monolith with separate service containers (service‑oriented architecture)

components.name: Vue Frontend
components.description: Vue 3 single‑page application that provides Player 1 UI for ship placement, board view and firing shots.

components.name: Game API Service
components.description: FastAPI service exposing HTTP endpoints for ship placement, firing, and board queries. Enforces turn rules and hides opponent ship positions.

components.name: MCP Tool Server
components.description: FastAPI service that wraps the same game actions behind the Model Context Protocol (MCP) SDK, allowing an AI agent to play via Streamable HTTP.

components.name: Game Logic Library
components.description: Pure Python package containing core Battleship rules: board representation, ship placement validation, hit/miss/sunk detection, and turn management. Holds the in‑memory game state.

architecture.dataFlow: The Vue SPA issues REST calls to the Game API Service for ship placement, shot firing, and board retrieval. It also calls the MCP Tool Server when an AI‑driven player is needed. Both API services delegate all game‑rule processing to the shared Game Logic Library, which updates the in‑memory game model and returns results. Responses are sent back to the UI, which renders the player's own board and the opponent‑view (hits/misses only).
integrations: Model Context Protocol (MCP) over Streamable HTTP
nonFunctional: Scalability – services are stateless; horizontal scaling possible via Docker Compose scaling if needed.
Security – no authentication required for the assignment; however, each service runs in its own container and does not expose opponent ship data.
Observability – standard Python logging to stdout; Docker captures logs for each container.
Fault tolerance – each request is isolated; loss of a container only affects the current game (in‑memory), which is acceptable for a prototype.
Maintainability – clear separation between UI, API, and pure domain logic enables easy future extensions.

techStack.rationale: Vue 3 offers a gentle learning curve, single‑file components, and built‑in reactivity that matches the simple UI needs. Vite provides fast dev server start‑up. React would add extra boilerplate (JSX, state management) for a small prototype, and Svelte, while lightweight, has a smaller ecosystem and fewer ready‑made UI components.

FastAPI gives automatic OpenAPI docs, async support, and type‑hint‑driven validation with minimal code—ideal for a quick REST service. Flask would require manual validation and documentation, while Django REST adds heavyweight ORM and project structure unnecessary for an in‑memory game.

alternatives: Node.js Express with custom MCP handling
Python Flask with manual MCP implementation
techStack.rationale: Using the same FastAPI stack keeps the codebase consistent and lets us reuse the Game Logic Library directly. Node.js would introduce a second language runtime for no benefit, and Flask would lack the built‑in request validation and async capabilities that FastAPI already provides.

alternatives: TypeScript shared library compiled to JavaScript
techStack.rationale: Python is already the language of the backend services, so a pure Python package avoids cross‑language integration overhead. TypeScript would require a build step and duplication of logic for the backend, while Rust adds compilation complexity unnecessary for a prototype.

Docker Compose is sufficient for a three‑service prototype, provides simple YAML configuration, and matches the assignment requirement of a single `docker compose up --build`. Swarm and Kubernetes add operational complexity that is not justified by the limited traffic and lack of persistence.

GitHub Actions integrates directly with the repository, requires no external server, and can run Docker builds and lint checks with minimal configuration. GitLab CI would need a separate GitLab instance, and Jenkins adds maintenance overhead.

pytest is the de‑facto standard for Python testing, offering simple fixtures and powerful assertions. Vitest aligns with Vite and provides fast, native ES module testing. unittest is more verbose, and Jest would require additional configuration for Vite. BDD tools are unnecessary for a short assignment.

techStack.choice: Standard logging to stdout (Python logging, console.log)
techStack.rationale: For a prototype, container stdout logs are sufficient and are captured automatically by Docker Compose. ELK and Prometheus add external services and configuration that are overkill for a short‑lived in‑memory game.

dbDesign.rationale: PostgreSQL provides strong ACID guarantees, rich data types, native UUID support, and powerful indexing options. It integrates seamlessly with FastAPI via async drivers (asyncpg) and fits the relational nature of the Battleship domain (players, games, ships, shots) while allowing future analytical queries (leaderboards, game statistics).

sampleQueries.description: Retrieve the opponent view for a given player (all shots fired at this player with hit/miss info).
sampleQueries.sql:
SELECT s.x, s.y, s.result, s.fired_at
FROM shots s
JOIN game_players gp ON s.game_id = gp.game_id
WHERE gp.player_id = $1
  AND s.target_player_id = $1
ORDER BY s.fired_at ASC;

sampleQueries.description: Get a player's own board: ship cells together with any shots that have hit them.
sampleQueries.sql:
SELECT sc.x, sc.y, s.result AS shot_result, s.fired_at
FROM ship_cells sc
JOIN ships sh ON sc.ship_id = sh.id
LEFT JOIN shots s ON s.game_id = sh.game_id
  AND s.target_player_id = sh.player_id
  AND s.x = sc.x AND s.y = sc.y
WHERE sh.game_id = $1 AND sh.player_id = $2
ORDER BY sc.x, sc.y;

sampleQueries.description: Calculate remaining (unsunk) ships per player in a game.
sampleQueries.sql:
WITH ship_hits AS (
  SELECT sh.id AS ship_id,
         COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE s.result IN ('hit','sunk')) AS hit_cells,
         sh.size
  FROM ships sh
  LEFT JOIN ship_cells sc ON sc.ship_id = sh.id
  LEFT JOIN shots s ON s.game_id = sh.game_id
    AND s.target_player_id = sh.player_id
    AND s.x = sc.x AND s.y = sc.y
  WHERE sh.game_id = $1
  GROUP BY sh.id
)
SELECT sh.player_id,
       COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE hit_cells < size) AS ships_remaining
FROM ships sh
JOIN ship_hits h ON h.ship_id = sh.id
GROUP BY sh.player_id;

SELECT p.id, p.name, COUNT(g.id) AS wins
FROM players p
JOIN games g ON g.winner_player_id = p.id
GROUP BY p.id, p.name
ORDER BY wins DESC;

sampleQueries.description: List all active (ongoing) games for a specific player.
sampleQueries.sql:
SELECT g.id, g.status, gp.player_number
FROM games g
JOIN game_players gp ON g.id = gp.game_id
WHERE gp.player_id = $1 AND g.status = 'ongoing'
ORDER BY g.created_at DESC;

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS games (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    status VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending' CHECK (status IN ('pending','ongoing','finished')),
    winner_player_id UUID REFERENCES players(id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS game_players (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    game_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES games(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    player_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES players(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    player_number INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (player_number IN (1,2)),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (game_id, player_number),
    UNIQUE (game_id, player_id)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ships (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    game_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES games(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    player_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES players(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    type VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL CHECK (type IN ('carrier','battleship','cruiser','submarine','destroyer')),
    size INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (size > 0),
    placed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ship_cells (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    ship_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES ships(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    x INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (x BETWEEN 0 AND 9),
    y INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (y BETWEEN 0 AND 9),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (ship_id, x, y)
);

CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS shots (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
    game_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES games(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    shooter_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES players(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    target_player_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES players(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    x INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (x BETWEEN 0 AND 9),
    y INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (y BETWEEN 0 AND 9),
    result VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL CHECK (result IN ('hit','miss','sunk')),
    fired_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    UNIQUE (game_id, shooter_id, x, y)
);

userStories.iWant: to place my ships on the board
userStories.soThat: I can set up my fleet before the game starts
acceptanceCriteria: The UI allows selecting a ship size (2, 3, 4) and dragging it onto board cells; placement is rejected if the ship would exceed board bounds or overlap another ship.
The backend endpoint POST /place_ship returns a success response for valid placements and an error with a clear message for invalid placements.
After a successful placement, the player's board view visually displays the ship positions.

userStories.iWant: to fire at opponent coordinates in turn
userStories.soThat: I can attempt to sink opponent ships
acceptanceCriteria: Clicking a cell on the opponent grid sends a shot request to POST /fire.
The backend enforces turn order and returns an error if it is not the player's turn.
The response indicates hit, miss, or sunk, and the UI updates the opponent view accordingly.

userStories.iWant: to view my own board and the opponent view (hits/misses only)
acceptanceCriteria: GET /board/{player_id} returns the full board with ship locations for the requesting player.
GET /opponent_view/{player_id} returns a masked board showing only hit/miss markers, never ship positions.
The frontend fetches these endpoints after each action and updates both grids correctly.

userStories.iWant: to invoke ship placement and firing via the MCP SDK
userStories.soThat: I can play the game programmatically
acceptanceCriteria: The MCP Tool Server exposes `place_ship` and `fire_shot` methods over Streamable HTTP.
A client using the Model Context Protocol SDK can call these methods and receives the same response schema as the REST API.
Invalid actions (e.g., out‑of‑bounds placement, firing out of turn) are returned as SDK errors with descriptive messages.

userStories.iWant: a responsive Vue SPA that shows my board, opponent view, and controls
userStories.soThat: I can interact with the game smoothly
acceptanceCriteria: The SPA loads with two 6×6 grids side‑by‑side.
Drag‑and‑drop ship placement works before the game starts and updates the board view.
After placement, clicking opponent cells fires shots, updates the view, and respects turn order until a win condition is reached.
When all opponent ships are sunk, a victory modal is displayed.

userStories.iWant: to launch the whole system with a single Docker Compose command
userStories.soThat: I can run the prototype locally with minimal effort
acceptanceCriteria: docker-compose.yml defines three services: frontend, api, mcp, each with its own build context.
Running `docker compose up --build` builds all images and starts containers without errors.
Containers communicate via the internal Docker network; the frontend can reach the API and MCP endpoints.

userStories.iWant: all game components (frontend SPA, Game API Service, MCP Tool Server, Domain Library) to be wired together so the game is playable end‑to‑end
userStories.soThat: I can experience a complete Battleship game without manual wiring
acceptanceCriteria: After `docker compose up`, opening the frontend URL loads the SPA and allows full gameplay: ship placement, turn‑based firing, and victory detection.
The SPA successfully calls the Game API Service for all actions; the MCP server runs and is reachable (though not required for manual play).
Docker logs show successful inter‑service communication and no unhandled exceptions.
An automated Cypress e2e test can complete a full game (place ships, fire shots, win) without page reloads.

comments.body: Only a health‑check test is present. The assignment requires pytest tests for the `place_ship` and `fire_shot` handlers. Add tests that verify successful ship placement, validation errors (e.g., mismatched coordinates count), and that `fire_shot` returns the expected schema. This is a **major** gap in test coverage.

The endpoint catches `ValidationError` manually, but FastAPI already converts Pydantic validation errors into 422 responses before the handler is called. The `try/except` block is redundant and can mask other exceptions. Consider removing it and letting FastAPI handle validation. This is a **minor** improvement.

The in‑memory `_game_board` is a module‑level mutable object shared across all requests and workers, which is not safe for concurrent usage. Use a FastAPI dependency (e.g., `Depends`) to provide a per‑request or thread‑safe board instance, or protect access with a lock. This is a **major** concern for production correctness.

The `FireShotRequest` model validates that `x` and `y` are non‑negative but does not enforce the board bounds (default 10x10). Add an upper bound (`lt=10`) to prevent out‑of‑range coordinates. This is a **minor** suggestion.

The `try/except` block catches `ValidationError`, but `Ship` is a plain dataclass, so no Pydantic validation occurs. This makes the exception handling unreachable and masks real errors. Remove the `ValidationError` catch (FastAPI already handles request validation) and let unexpected errors propagate as 500 responses, or raise appropriate HTTP errors where needed.

`Board.place_ship` currently appends ships without any validation (bounds, overlap, size vs coordinates). This allows invalid game state and defeats the purpose of the domain library. Implement proper validation or at least raise a clear exception for out‑of‑bounds or overlapping placements; otherwise the MCP handlers may store illegal ships.

comments.body: This PR adds only a mission report and does not include the required PlayerBoard.vue component or any related Vue code. Please implement the component according to the project's Vue conventions before merging.
Similarly, this file only documents a missing Python implementation. The POST /place_ship endpoint and its validation logic need to be added to the FastAPI service with proper tests.

The repository appears to be missing the core source directories and convention files referenced in the review guidelines (e.g., .conventions/Angular.md, .conventions/React.md, etc.). Ensure the project scaffolding is present so that code can be reviewed against the established standards.
Missing import for `HTTPException`. Import it from `fastapi` and use it for validation errors instead of raising a generic `Exception`.
Raising a generic `Exception` on validation failure results in a 500 response. Replace with `raise HTTPException(status_code=422, detail=str(e))` to return proper FastAPI validation errors.

The endpoint signature `async def place_ship(payload: Dict)` bypasses FastAPI's request‑body parsing. Define a Pydantic model (e.g., `PlaceShipRequest`) and use it as the parameter type to get automatic validation and clearer API contracts.

The test calls `app.post('/place_ship')(payload)`, which invokes the decorator rather than the registered handler. Use FastAPI's `TestClient` (or the stub's `app.routes['/place_ship'](payload)`) to invoke the endpoint correctly.

The CSS grid uses `repeat(var(--size), 30px)` but the `--size` CSS variable is never defined, resulting in a grid with zero columns. Bind the grid size via a style attribute, e.g., `:style="{'--size': props.size}"` or compute the `grid-template-columns` directly in the component.

When a diagonal selection is made, `generateCoordinates` silently falls back to a single cell. This hides user errors. Consider raising an error or emitting a validation event instead of silently correcting the input.

PlaceShipRequest inherits from the stub BaseModel but does not declare any fields (e.g., __fields__ = ['coordinates']). As a result, required‑field validation never runs, allowing malformed payloads to pass. Define the required fields or adjust the stub to perform proper validation.

When validation fails you raise HTTPException, but the FastAPI stub's TestClient does not catch this exception and will propagate it, causing the request to crash instead of returning a 422 response. Modify the endpoint to return an error object (e.g., {detail: ...}) or adapt the TestClient stub to handle HTTPException.

generateCoordinates emits an 'invalid-placement' event for diagonal selections but still returns an empty array, and the caller later emits a 'place-ship' event with that empty array. This results in a misleading 'place-ship' emission. Return early after emitting the invalid event or have the caller check for an empty array before emitting.

Two separate stub implementations of FastAPI (`fastapi/__init__.py` and `fastapi/testclient.py`) exist. This duplication can cause maintenance overhead and subtle inconsistencies. After a successful placement, update the `hasShip` flag on the involved cells so the UI reflects the placed ship (e.g., iterate over `coordinates` and set `cell.hasShip = true`). This improves user feedback.

Consider making `selected` a reactive `ref([])` instead of a plain array. While the current logic works, a reactive reference would allow future UI updates (e.g., highlighting selected cells) without additional work.

The `place_ship` endpoint should accept a `PlaceShipRequest` model directly (e.g., `def place_ship(request: PlaceShipRequest):`). This enables FastAPI's automatic request validation, OpenAPI schema generation, and clearer type hints.

After successful validation the endpoint should invoke the domain library's ship‑placement function (e.g., `game_service.place_ship(validated)`), and handle any domain errors. Returning only the validated payload bypasses business logic.

Clicking the same cell twice results in a single‑coordinate ship being emitted, which the backend rejects. Add a check to prevent duplicate selections and emit an `invalid-placement` event (or ignore the second click).
`selected` is a plain array; consider making it a reactive `ref([])` so future UI updates (e.g., highlighting selected cells) work without extra work.

The `place_ship` endpoint expects a `PlaceShipRequest` model instance, but the FastAPI stub's `TestClient` calls the handler with a plain dict, leading to an AttributeError (`request.coordinates`). comments.body: File src/components/OpponentBoard.vue does not exist or contains no changes. The story requires a new OpponentBoard component with click‑to‑fire functionality and proper event emission. Add the component implementation and corresponding tests.

The `size` prop has no default value. If the component is used without explicitly providing `size`, the computed `cells` loop will throw because `props.size` is undefined. Add a sensible default (e.g., 10) and validate that it is a positive integer.

The `Board` class repeats attribute definitions and methods after the first `place_ship` implementation, creating duplicate code and potential confusion. Remove the duplicated docstring, attribute declarations, and methods so the class is defined only once.

The `get` method contains dead code after the `return decorator` statement, including an unrelated POST‑route registration block. This unreachable code should be removed to keep the stub clean and avoid accidental side‑effects.

The `/fire` endpoint does not validate that the supplied `x` and `y` coordinates are within the board dimensions (`_game_board.width` / `height`). Out‑of‑range coordinates could be accepted silently. Add a check and raise a 400 error if coordinates are outside the board.

The endpoint uses module‑level mutable globals (`_game_board`, `_current_turn`) without any concurrency protection. In a real server this could cause race conditions. Consider encapsulating state in a thread‑safe service or using dependency injection.

The `cells` computed returns plain objects and you mutate `hasShip` directly. This mutation won't trigger UI updates because the objects aren't reactive. Consider storing cell state in a `ref`/`reactive` collection or managing ship positions separately to ensure the board reflects changes.

`generateCoordinates` emits validation events directly. For clearer separation of concerns, let the function only return coordinates (or an empty array) and handle validation/emission in `onCellClick`.

The `result` field of `FireShotResponse` is a free‑form string. Using an `Enum` (e.g., `class ShotResult(str, Enum): HIT = "hit"; MISS = "miss"`) would make the API contract stricter and self‑documenting.
Turn enforcement is hard‑coded to player 1. If the game expands to multiple players, consider passing a player identifier in the request payload and validating against `_current_turn`.
The CSS grid uses a fixed `30px` cell size. Exposing this as a CSS variable or component prop would make the board more flexible for different screen sizes.

The `Board.ships` annotation uses the `|` union syntax, which requires Python 3.10+. Add `from __future__ import annotations` at the top for forward‑compatible type hints if the project may run on earlier versions.

The module uses global mutable variables (`_game_board`, `_current_turn`) to store game state. In a real FastAPI deployment with multiple workers or async requests this can cause race conditions and inconsistent state. Refactor to use a proper state manager (e.g., dependency‑injected singleton, database, or in‑memory store with locks).

`Board.ships` is typed with the union operator (`List[Ship] | None`), which requires Python 3.10+. If the project needs to support earlier versions, add `from __future__ import annotations` at the top or use `Optional[List[Ship]]`. This prevents import errors in environments with older interpreters.

The cell elements are clickable but lack accessibility attributes. Add `role="button"` and an appropriate `aria-label` (e.g., `aria-label="Fire at ${cell.x}, ${cell.y}"`) so screen readers can convey the action to users with disabilities.

Tests manipulate internal globals (`_game_board`, `_current_turn`) directly. This couples the test suite to implementation details and bypasses the public API. Consider adding API endpoints or service methods to set up board state, and use those in tests to keep the contract‑driven testing approach.

The `FireShotResponse` model defines `result` as a free‑form string. Using an `Enum` (e.g., `class ShotResult(str, Enum): HIT = "hit"; MISS = "miss"`) would make the response schema explicit and help client code with type safety.

Turn enforcement is hard‑coded to player 1. If the game expands to multiple players, the endpoint should accept a player identifier in the request payload and validate it against the current turn, rather than relying on a fixed constant.

The `/reset`, `/place_ships`, and `/set_turn` endpoints are intended only for tests but are publicly reachable. Exposing them in production allows anyone to manipulate game state, which is a security risk. Move these helpers to a test‑only module or protect them with authentication/authorization.
There is a duplicate import of `BaseModel` and the globals `_game_board` and `_current_turn` are unused. Remove the redundant import and dead code to keep the module clean and avoid confusion.

Each cell is rendered with `role="button"` but lacks `tabindex="0"` (or a Vue `v-bind` for focusability). Without it, keyboard users cannot navigate to the cells. Add `tabindex="0"` and handle `keydown` events for accessibility.

The `size` prop validator only checks for a positive integer. Extremely large values could cause the browser to render an enormous grid, degrading performance. Consider adding an upper bound (e.g., max 20) or sanitizing the prop before rendering.
`os` is used before it is imported, and `router` is referenced before it is defined. This will raise a NameError at import time, breaking the service and all tests.

The conditional `if os.getenv("TEST_MODE") == "true": app.include_router(router)` runs before `router` is defined. Move the router definition (and the `import os`) above this block and include the router after it is created.

Test utility routes (`/reset`, `/place_ships`, `/set_turn`) are attached to `router` but the router is only included when `TEST_MODE` env var is true. The test suite does not set this variable, resulting in 404 errors. Include the router unconditionally for test environments or adjust the test setup to set `TEST_MODE=true`.

`ShipInput.coordinates` is typed as `list[tuple[int, int]]` while the test payload sends a list of lists (e.g., `[[1,1],[1,2]]`). Pydantic may not coerce this correctly. Change the type to `List[List[int]]` or add a validator that converts inner lists to tuples.
Import order should follow the project's Python conventions: standard library imports (`os`, `enum`) first, then third‑party (`fastapi`, `pydantic`), then local modules. Reorder imports accordingly.
The component emits a `fire` event but does not prevent multiple rapid clicks on the same cell, which could lead to duplicate shots. Consider disabling the cell or debouncing the click handler.

The `/fire` endpoint is defined directly on the FastAPI `app` while other endpoints use the `router`. This inconsistency can lead to fragmented OpenAPI docs and makes future route grouping harder. Move the `@app.post("/fire")` handler to the `router` (e.g., `@router.post("/fire")`).

`ShipInput.coordinates` is typed as `List[List[int]]` but there is no validation that each inner list contains exactly two integers. Malformed payloads could raise runtime errors when converting to tuples. Add a Pydantic validator to ensure each coordinate pair has length 2 and contains integers.

The component tracks fired cells internally but does not provide any visual or ARIA feedback (e.g., `aria-pressed` or a CSS class) to indicate a cell has already been fired. This reduces accessibility and user experience. Add a state‑based class and appropriate ARIA attribute to convey the disabled/fired state.

`GameState` is implemented as a process‑wide singleton. While acceptable for a prototype, in a real deployment this would cause race conditions and state leakage across users. Document this limitation and consider refactoring to a per‑session or database‑backed store before production.

Tests cover hit, miss, and turn validation but miss edge‑case validation for out‑of‑bounds coordinates. Add a test that posts a shot with coordinates outside the board and expects a 400 response with "Coordinates out of bounds".

`Board.ships` is typed as `Optional[List[Ship]]` but is always initialized to an empty list in `__post_init__`. The type hint should be `List[Ship]` to reflect actual usage and avoid unnecessary `None` handling.

comments.body: The `src/api/client.ts` module referenced in the PR description is absent from the diff. A Pinia store (`gameStore`) that holds the board state, current turn, and actions invoking the API client is missing. Implement the store according to the architecture guidelines and ensure it is registered in `src/main.ts`.
The component appears to render the board but does not import or use the `gameStore` actions to fetch board data or submit moves. Wire the component to the store so that it reflects real game state.

A Pinia store (`gameStore`) is not present. Create the store to manage board state, current turn, and actions that call the API client, and register it in `src/main.ts`.

The component renders the board but does not interact with the game store to fetch board data or dispatch ship placement actions. Wire it to the store to reflect real game state and trigger API calls.
The modal emits a `restart` event but no store action is connected to actually reset the game. Add a method that dispatches the appropriate store reset action and ensure the button triggers it.
Tests cover UI interactions but lack unit tests for the API client functions and Pinia store actions. Add test suites that mock Axios responses and verify state updates to ensure full coverage.
The added `index.html` does not follow the project's Vite template conventions (missing script tags, proper root element). Align it with the standard Vite entry point to avoid build/runtime issues.

The test imports `apiClient` before mocking `axios`. Because `apiClient` creates its own Axios instance at import time, the subsequent `vi.mock('axios')` does not affect the already‑created instance, causing real HTTP calls and test failures. Move the `vi.mock('axios')` call to a separate module that mocks before importing `apiClient`, or refactor `client.ts` to export a factory function that can be injected with a mocked Axios instance.

`emit('place-ship', { coordinates })` is used but the event is not declared in `defineEmits`. This results in a TypeScript error and breaks strict typing. Add the event to the emits definition, e.g., `defineEmits<{ (e: 'place-ship', payload: { coordinates: Coordinate[] }): void; (e: 'invalid-placement', payload: { message: string }): void; }>();`.

`useGameStore` is imported but never used in the component (the store reset is called via a local `useGameStore()` inside `onRestart`). Remove the unused import or use the imported instance to avoid lint warnings.

The `BoardCell` interface is duplicated here and also defined in `src/api/client.ts`. Keeping a single source of truth prevents type drift. Consider importing the type from the client module instead of redefining it.

The `ApiClient` constructor defaults `baseURL` to an empty string. In production this may lead to requests to the wrong origin. Provide a sensible default (e.g., read from an environment variable) or require the caller to pass the base URL explicitly.

The `generateCoordinates` function returns an empty array when a diagonal placement is attempted, but the calling code still proceeds to call `gameStore.placeShip` after checking `coordinates.length > 0`. Ensure that invalid placements are fully aborted and provide user feedback, otherwise a ship could be placed with no coordinates silently.

The `placeShip` method returns a `BoardResponse` with a `cells` array, but the backend `/games/{gameId}/ships` endpoint (not shown) and the `getBoard` endpoint return objects containing `width`, `height`, and `ships`. This type mismatch will cause undefined `cells` at runtime. Align the client response type with the actual backend payload or transform the data in the client.

`fireShot` suffers the same contract mismatch as `placeShip`; the backend returns a board description (width/height/ships) while the client expects `BoardResponse` with `cells`. Update the method signature or map the response to the expected shape.

`getBoard` currently returns a `BoardResponse` (cells only) but the FastAPI `GET /board/{player_id}` endpoint returns `width`, `height`, and a list of `ships`. This will break the store that expects `cells`. Refactor either the endpoint to return `cells` or adjust the client to handle the full board object.

`getOpponentView` is typed to return `BoardResponse`, yet the backend `GET /opponent_view/{player_id}` returns `{ width, height, hits, misses }`. The client will receive `undefined` for `cells`. Define a proper `OpponentViewResponse` type and update the store accordingly.

The test suite does not include a test for `getOpponentView`. Add a unit test that mocks the Axios GET call and verifies the method returns the correctly typed data, ensuring full coverage of the client API.

The `Board` dataclass uses the Python 3.10 union syntax (`List[Ship] | None`). If the runtime environment uses an earlier Python version, this will raise a syntax error. Replace with `Optional[List[Ship]]` from `typing` for broader compatibility.

The `getBoard` method declares a return type of `BoardInfoResponse` but uses the generic `BoardResponse` which is not defined anywhere. This will cause a TypeScript compilation error. Change the generic to `BoardInfoResponse` (or import the correct type) and ensure the response shape matches the interface.

Similarly, `getOpponentView` uses the undefined generic `BoardResponse` while the method returns `OpponentViewResponse`. Update the generic to `OpponentViewResponse` to align with the declared return type.

The store imports `BoardResponse` from `../api/client`, but that type does not exist. This import will fail and break the store. Replace it with the correct `BoardInfoResponse` (or the appropriate type) and adjust any usages accordingly.

The `fireShot` action assigns `this.opponentBoard = this.transformOpponentViewFromBoardInfo(res);` but `transformOpponentViewFromBoardInfo` currently just reuses `transformBoardInfo`, which treats ship cells as opponent view cells. This is semantically incorrect and will display ships on the opponent board. Implement a proper conversion that maps hits/misses from the shot response, or adjust the API to return an `OpponentViewResponse` for shots.

The test suite re‑mocks `axios.create` inside each test, but `apiClient` is instantiated at import time using the first mock. Subsequent `mockReturnValue` calls do not affect the already‑created instance, so the expectations (`expect(postMock).toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)`) will always fail. Refactor the tests to mock the instance *before* importing `apiClient` and reuse the same mocked instance for all assertions, or expose a way to inject a mock http client.
There is no test for the `getOpponentView` method, leaving that API path unverified. Add a test case that mocks a GET request and asserts the correct endpoint and response handling.

The client module does not export a type named `BoardResponse`, yet `src/store/gameStore.ts` imports it. This will cause a compile‑time error. Either rename `BoardInfoResponse` to `BoardResponse` and export it, or add an explicit `export type BoardResponse = BoardInfoResponse;` alias.

`BoardInfoResponse` is defined with `width`, `height`, and `ships`, but the test suite (and likely the backend) expects a `cells` array in the response. The shape mismatch will break type checking and runtime data handling. Align the interface with the actual API payload (e.g., add `cells: BoardCell[]` or adjust the tests/backend to use `ships`).

`getOpponentView` uses the endpoint `/games/${gameId}/opponent-board`, which does not match the specification (`GET /opponent_view/{player_id}`). This will result in 404 errors. Update the URL to the correct path and ensure the parameter name (`player_id` vs `gameId`) aligns with the backend contract.

`fetchBoard` performs two sequential API calls (`getBoard` then `getOpponentView`). They are independent and can be fetched in parallel with `Promise.all` to reduce latency. Refactor to run them concurrently and handle errors appropriately.

`transformBoardInfo` only creates cells for ship positions, omitting empty cells. The UI may rely on a full board matrix to render hits/misses correctly. Consider generating a complete grid based on `width`/`height` and marking ship cells, empty cells, and later hit/miss states.

The component imports `useGameStore` solely to call `resetGame` on restart. This creates an unnecessary store dependency for a presentational component. Emit the `restart` event and let the parent handle store reset, keeping the modal decoupled.

Export a `BoardResponse` interface that matches the shape used in tests (e.g. `{ cells: BoardCell[] }`) and update `placeShip`, `fireShot`, and `getBoard` to return this type. Currently they return `BoardInfoResponse` which lacks a `cells` property, causing a type mismatch with the test suite.

`BoardResponse` is imported from `../api/client` but that type does not exist. After adding the proper export in `client.ts`, import it here (or remove the import if you decide to keep using `BoardInfoResponse`). This compile error blocks the build.

The helper `transformOpponentViewFromBoardInfo` simply re‑uses `transformBoardInfo`, which is incorrect for the fire‑shot response. Implement a proper conversion that extracts hit/miss coordinates from the API response (or change the API to return an `OpponentViewResponse`).

The mocked Axios responses use a `{ cells: [...] }` payload, but the client methods are typed to return `BoardInfoResponse`. Update the test to reflect the actual return type (`BoardResponse`) or adjust the client implementation to return the `cells` field as defined in the test.

The `BoardCell` interface includes an optional `hit` flag but no explicit `hasShip` default for empty cells. Consider adding a `hasShip: false` default when constructing opponent view cells to avoid undefined values.

The component emits a `restart` event but also directly resets the store. This double‑reset can cause unexpected side‑effects if a parent also handles the event. Choose either to emit and let the parent reset, or handle the reset internally, but avoid doing both.

Export a `BoardResponse` interface that includes a `cells: BoardCell[]` property (e.g., `{ cells: BoardCell[] }`). The current client methods (`placeShip`, `fireShot`, `getBoard`) return `BoardInfoResponse`, which lacks this field and causes type mismatches with the test suite and store.

`fireShot` is typed to return `BoardInfoResponse`, but the API spec (and the store) expect an opponent‑view style response. Change the return type to `OpponentViewResponse` (or the newly added `BoardResponse`) and adjust the implementation accordingly.

The URL used in `getOpponentView` (`/games/${gameId}/opponent-board`) does not match the backend route (`/opponent_view/{player_id}`). Update the endpoint to the correct path to avoid 404 errors at runtime.

The test suite mocks `axios.create` after the `apiClient` instance has already been constructed (imported earlier). Re‑mocking `axios.create` does not replace the internal `http` instance, so the mocked responses are never used. Refactor the test to either inject a mock http client into `ApiClient` or recreate the client after setting the mock implementation.

The `BoardResponse` interface only defines `cells`, but the store expects properties like `ships`, `hits`, and `misses`. Either extend `BoardResponse` to include those fields or create distinct response interfaces that match the backend contract. This mismatch will cause TypeScript compile errors and runtime failures.

`BoardInfoResponse` and `OpponentViewResponse` are type aliases of `BoardResponse`, yet they are used to represent different payload shapes. Define proper interfaces for each response type instead of aliasing to avoid incorrect typings throughout the codebase.

The store imports only `BoardResponse` and `BoardCell` but later references `BoardInfoResponse` and `OpponentViewResponse`, which are not imported. This results in a TypeScript "cannot find name" error. Import the correct types from `../api/client` or adjust the code to use the imported types.

`transformBoardInfo` accesses `info.ships`, but the `BoardResponse` (or the aliased type) does not contain a `ships` array. Update the transformation logic to match the actual response shape (e.g., iterate over `info.cells` or define a proper `BoardInfoResponse` interface with `ships`).

`transformOpponentView` expects `view.hits` and `view.misses`, which are not present in the current response type. Align this method with the real opponent view payload or adjust the API client to return an object with those arrays.
Tests cover `placeShip`, `fireShot`, and `getBoard` but omit `getOpponentView`. Add a test case for `getOpponentView` to ensure the correct endpoint and response handling are verified.

The endpoint URLs (`/games/${gameId}/board` and `/games/${gameId}/opponent-board`) do not match the backend routes (`/board/{player_id}` and `/opponent_view/{player_id}`). Align the client paths with the server API to avoid 404 errors.

The PR does not include any Pinia store setup. Create a store (e.g., useGameStore) that holds game state (ships, hits, etc.) and provide it in main.ts. This is required by the architecture and the description.

Axios base URL and the Game API Service are referenced in the description but no Axios configuration or service files are present. Add an Axios instance with the base URL (from env) and export functions used by components.
VictoryModal component is mentioned in the task but never imported or used. Implement the modal component (or import it if already existing) and integrate it to display when the game is won.

App.vue directly accesses the store and sets winner via a simple if‑statement; this runs only once on component init and will not react to future store changes. Use a watch on store.winner (as done in Game.vue) or computed property to keep UI in sync.

Axios base URL is set globally, but the project expects a dedicated Axios instance exported from src/services/api.ts. Creating the instance here couples configuration to the app bootstrap and makes testing harder. Refactor to use the exported instance and ensure environment variables are typed.

Router defines only the root route to GameView; the VictoryModal component is imported but never used in routes, and there is no fallback or 404 route. Add a route for the victory screen or embed it within GameView as a modal, and include a catch‑all route.

The store defines a custom $reset method but does not follow Pinia's built‑in reset pattern. Expose reset via store.$reset = () => { ... } or use defineStore's built‑in reset functionality. Also, the winner detection logic is simplistic and may set winner on any 'win' hit without verifying all ships are sunk.

Service functions lack error handling; any network failure will throw uncaught promises in components. Wrap axios calls in try/catch and return a typed result or throw a custom error to be handled by UI.

Game.vue duplicates the layout already present in App.vue, leading to two separate instances of PlayerBoard and OpponentBoard. Choose a single source of truth (either App.vue or a dedicated route view) to avoid UI duplication and state inconsistencies.

The `shipCells` ref holds a `Set`, but the template accesses it as `shipCells.has(cell.id)`. Since `shipCells` is a ref, you need to use `shipCells.value.has(...)` (or expose a computed wrapper) for Vue to track changes. As written, ship cells will never update in the UI, causing a major functional bug.

Ship placement does not check whether the new ship overlaps any existing ship cells. Overlapping placements should be rejected and emit an `invalid-placement` event. Add a validation step before emitting `place-ship`.

The `onFire` handler randomly returns `'hit'` or `'miss'` and never returns `'win'`. Consequently the store's win‑detection logic never runs, and the `VictoryModal` will never appear. Replace the placeholder with a real API call (`fireShot`) and handle the server‑provided result.

The win detection only checks for `hit.result === 'win'` and then compares hit count to total ship cells. This logic is fragile and tied to a specific payload shape. Consider moving win detection to the backend and expose a dedicated endpoint, or at least make the client logic more robust (e.g., track ship health).

Error handling rethrows a generic `Error` losing the original stack trace and any response details (status code, payload). Preserve the original error or create a custom error type that includes `error.response?.data` for better UI diagnostics.

There are no unit tests covering the Pinia store's logic (ship addition, hit recording, win detection). Add tests to ensure the store behaves correctly, especially edge cases like overlapping ships and win conditions.

`shipCells` is a ref, but the template accesses it directly as `shipCells.value.has(cell.id)`. Vue will not track changes, causing ship cells to never update in the UI. Use a computed wrapper or access `.value` in the template.
Ship placement does not check for overlap with existing ships before emitting `place-ship`. This can lead to invalid game state. Add overlap validation and emit `invalid-placement` when detected.

The `onFire` handler assumes the API returns a `result` field but does not handle possible error shapes or missing data, and it silently logs errors. Improve error handling and ensure the response format is validated before updating the store.

Error handling in `fireShot` and other functions wraps the original error in a generic `Error`, losing stack trace and response details. Preserve the original error or create a custom error type that includes `error.response` data for better diagnostics.

The Pinia store lacks unit tests covering ship addition, hit recording, and win detection. Add comprehensive tests to verify correct behavior, especially edge cases like overlapping ships and win conditions.

The component does not expose any props or slots for customizing cell size or styling beyond the default, limiting reusability. Consider adding a `cellSize` prop and using CSS variables for better flexibility.

The Axios instance posts to `/games/${gameId}/shots`, but the backend Game API defines the fire endpoint as `POST /fire` (no gameId segment). This mismatch will cause 404 errors at runtime. Update either the backend route to include the gameId path or adjust the frontend to call the correct `/fire` endpoint.

`fireShot` returns `response.data` which is expected to contain a `result` string. The backend `FireShotResponse` returns `result` as an enum (`"hit"` or `"miss"`). The store's win detection checks for `result === 'win'`, which will never be true. Either extend the backend to return a `'win'` result when appropriate, or modify the frontend/store logic to derive a win condition from hit counts.

The store manually defines a `$reset` method, but Pinia already provides a built‑in `$reset` for setup stores. Overriding it can cause confusion and may break future Pinia upgrades. Remove the custom `$reset` and rely on Pinia's native reset functionality.

`onFire` catches errors and sets `errorMessage`, but it also logs the error to the console. In production, consider using a proper logging service instead of `console.error` to avoid leaking sensitive information.

The `place_ships` endpoint accepts a list of `ShipInput` objects but does not validate ship size against the board or check for overlapping ships. Add validation to enforce game rules and return appropriate HTTP errors for invalid placements.

`fire_shot` toggles the turn without persisting any game state beyond the in‑memory `GameState`. For a real deployment, consider persisting state (e.g., in a database) or at least documenting that this is a demo implementation.

The Axios POST URL `/games/${gameId}/shots` does not match the backend endpoint which expects `POST /fire` (no gameId segment). This will cause 404 errors at runtime. Align the frontend call with the backend route or update the backend to include the gameId path.

`fireShot` returns `response.data` expecting a `result` string, but the backend returns an enum (`"hit"` or `"miss"`). The store checks for `result === 'win'`, which will never be true, breaking win detection. Adjust the frontend to handle the enum or extend the backend to return a `'win'` result when appropriate.

Ship placement logic does not validate ship size against allowed limits or ensure ships are placed within board bounds, leading to potential invalid game states. Add validation for ship length and board boundaries, and emit appropriate error events.

When a ship placement overlaps an existing ship, the code emits an `invalid-placement` event but still proceeds to update `shipCells` after the overlap check due to missing early return. This can cause overlapping ships to be displayed. Ensure the function returns early after emitting the overlap error.

`onFire` uses a hard‑coded `gameId = 'demo-game'`. In a real application the game ID should be managed by the store or route parameters. Using a static ID prevents multiple games and breaks consistency with backend state.

The store file could not be loaded for review, but prior comments indicated a custom `$reset` method overriding Pinia's built‑in reset. Remove the custom implementation and rely on Pinia's native `$reset` to avoid future compatibility issues.
The `/place_ships` endpoint accepts arbitrary ship data without validating ship size, orientation, overlap, or board boundaries. Add comprehensive validation to prevent invalid game states.
The `/fire` endpoint toggles `current_turn` without persisting shot results or checking for game over conditions. Implement proper turn management and win detection logic.

The FastAPI app exposes mutable global state (`GameState`) without any authentication or rate limiting, creating a security risk. Introduce auth (e.g., API keys) and consider per‑session state storage.

The frontend API client constructs URLs like `/games/${gameId}/ships` which do not correspond to any defined backend routes, causing runtime 404 errors. Align the client endpoints with the actual FastAPI routes or add the missing routes.
Error handling re‑throws the raw Axios error, leaking potentially sensitive information to the UI. Wrap errors in a sanitized error object before throwing.

The router test only checks for the existence of the Game route but does not verify that the NotFound catch‑all works or that navigation resolves correctly. Add tests for the NotFound route and navigation behavior.

Calling `useRoute()` inside the `onFire` handler violates Vue's Composition API rules – composables should be invoked at the top level of `setup`. Move `const route = useRoute();` outside of the function and reuse the route object.

`fireShot` is invoked without a `gameId` argument, but the backend API expects a game identifier in the request URL. This will cause 404 errors at runtime. Pass the `gameId` (or adjust the service to match the backend contract).

This mismatch can produce misaligned cells when a custom `cellSize` prop is provided. Replace the hard‑coded value with `var(--cell-size)`.

The `NotFound` component is imported but not given a default export in its file (`NotFound.vue`). Ensure the component uses `export default` or adjust the import to match the component's export style to avoid runtime errors.

The store file was not reviewed due to tool limits, but ensure it defines a `winner` state property, provides a `$reset` method, and is correctly typed according to the project's TypeScript conventions. Missing or incorrectly typed store logic can break the `Game.vue` watch logic.

The fireShot function signature expects (gameId: string, payload: FirePayload, playerId?: number) but is called in Game.vue with only a payload. This will cause a runtime error. Update the function signature or adjust the call to include the required gameId parameter.
The route variable is redeclared inside onFire, shadowing the outer const and causing confusion. Remove the inner declaration and use the existing route constant.

The router instance is imported directly, but the test environment may need to install Pinia or other plugins. Ensure the router is created with the necessary app context or mock the plugins appropriately.
State is stored in refs but not persisted; a page reload will lose game progress. Consider using Pinia's persisted state plugin or localStorage to retain state across sessions.
The Pinia store is created but not provided to the app before mounting. While app.use(createPinia()) works, ensure any plugins that rely on the store are registered after the store is attached.
The router is exported as default but not typed; consider exporting a typed const for better type safety and to aid test imports.

The fireShot function signature includes a gameId parameter that is never used in the request payload, and the function is called elsewhere without providing this argument. This mismatch leads to TypeScript errors and unclear API contract. Refactor the function to either require and include gameId in the request URL/body or remove the parameter entirely.

The file imports 'ref' twice (once in the combined import statement and again later). This redundant import is unnecessary and should be cleaned up for clarity.

The grid CSS uses a fixed 30px column size (grid-template-columns: repeat(var(--size), 30px)) while the cell size is set via the '--cell-size' variable. If the cellSize prop changes, column width will not reflect it, causing layout inconsistencies. Use var(--cell-size) for the column size as well.

Error handling in the API helpers discards the original error information, throwing a generic message. Preserve the original error details (e.g., include error.response?.data) to aid debugging and provide more useful feedback to callers.
